---
title: Pipes and Filters
---

Every command we have used so far prints its answer on the screen. We have seen
one other place that answer can go: `>` sends it into a file instead.

This chapter is about a third place it can go - into another command.

In this chapter, we'll learn about:

* `|` - the pipe, which joins two commands together

We'll use `figlet` and `cowsay` from the previous chapter to see what that
means, because both of them do something you can see at a glance.

## Commands we already know

Here is `echo`, from the first chapter:

```session
$ echo hello
hello
```

And here is `date`:

```session
$ date
Mon Aug 17 01:20:29 UTC 2026
```

And here is `figlet`, which we installed in the previous chapter. Give it a
word and it prints that word in large letters:

```session
$ figlet hello
 _          _ _
| |__   ___| | | ___
| '_ \ / _ \ | |/ _ \
| | | |  __/ | | (_) |
|_| |_|\___|_|_|\___/

```

Three separate commands, each printing its own answer to the screen.

## Joining two commands

Now type this:

```session
$ echo hello | figlet
 _          _ _
| |__   ___| | | ___
| '_ \ / _ \ | |/ _ \
| | | |  __/ | | (_) |
|_| |_|\___|_|_|\___/

```

The same large `hello`, but we got there a different way. The `|` character is
called a **pipe**. It says: take the output of the command on the left, and
give it to the command on the right, instead of printing it on the screen.

So `echo hello` printed nothing where we could see it. Its output went into
`figlet`, and what we saw was `figlet`'s output.

::: {.callout-tip}
The `|` character is usually on the same key as `\`, above the Enter key. The
two share a key, so you have to hold **Shift** to get the `|`. It is a
vertical bar, not the letter `l` or a capital `I`.
:::

Read a pipeline from left to right, the way you would read a sentence: run
`echo hello`, then hand the result to `figlet`.

## Why that is useful

Piping `echo hello` into `figlet` is a roundabout way of doing something we
could already do by typing `figlet hello`. But the left of the pipe can be any
command at all, and most commands print something we do not know in advance.

`date` is one of them. We do not know what the time is until we ask, so we
could not have typed it into `figlet` ourselves. With a pipe we do not need to
- we hand `date`'s answer straight across:

```session
$ date | figlet
 __  __                  _                 _ _____
|  \/  | ___  _ __      / \  _   _  __ _  / |___  |
| |\/| |/ _ \| '_ \    / _ \| | | |/ _` | | |  / /
| |  | | (_) | | | |  / ___ \ |_| | (_| | | | / /
|_|  |_|\___/|_| |_| /_/   \_\__,_|\__, | |_|/_/
                                   |___/
  ___  _   ____   ___    ____ ____    _   _ _____ ____
 / _ \/ |_|___ \ / _ \ _| ___|___ \  | | | |_   _/ ___|
| | | | (_) __) | | | (_)___ \ __) | | | | | | || |
| |_| | |_ / __/| |_| |_ ___) / __/  | |_| | | || |___
 \___/|_(_)_____|\___/(_)____/_____|  \___/  |_| \____|

 ____   ___ ____   __
|___ \ / _ \___ \ / /_
  __) | | | |__) | '_ \
 / __/| |_| / __/| (_) |
|_____|\___/_____|\___/

```

The date and time, in letters big enough to read across the room. `figlet` had
no idea where the text came from, and `date` had no idea where its answer was
going. Neither command was written with the other in mind.

The text on the left can be as long as you like. `seq 5` prints five lines, so
`figlet` gets five lines and draws each one:

```session
$ seq 5 | figlet
 _
/ |
| |
| |
|_|

 ____
|___ \
  __) |
 / __/
|_____|

 _____
|___ /
  |_ \
 ___) |
|____/

 _  _
| || |
| || |_
|__   _|
   |_|

 ____
| ___|
|___ \
 ___) |
|____/

```

The right of the pipe is just as free. `figlet` is not special - anything that
reads text will do, and `cowsay` reads text too:

```session
$ date | cowsay
 ______________________________
< Mon Aug 17 01:23:22 UTC 2026 >
 ------------------------------
        \   ^__^
         \  (oo)\_______
            (__)\       )\/\
                ||----w |
                ||     ||

```

We changed the command on the right and got a completely different result,
without touching the command on the left. That is the arrangement worth
noticing: each command does one thing, and the pipe decides what is joined to
what.

## Piping one into the other

Both of our commands produce text, and both of them read text. So we can join
them to each other:

```session
$ figlet hello | cowsay
 ________________________________________
/  _ _ _ | |__ ___| | | ___ | '_ \ / _ \ \
| | |/ _ \ | | | | __/ | | (_) | |_|     |
\ |_|\___|_|_|\___/                      /
 ----------------------------------------
        \   ^__^
         \  (oo)\_______
            (__)\       )\/\
                ||----w |
                ||     ||
```

That is a mess, and it is worth understanding why. `cowsay` expects a sentence,
so it rearranges the words to fit a tidy speech bubble - it runs lines together
and breaks them wherever the bubble ends. That is helpful for a sentence, but
it destroys a picture.

`cowsay -n` turns that rearranging off, leaving the text exactly as it arrived:

```session
$ figlet hello | cowsay -n
 ________________________
/  _          _ _        \
| | |__   ___| | | ___   |
| | '_ \ / _ \ | |/ _ \  |
| | | | |  __/ | | (_) | |
| |_| |_|\___|_|_|\___/  |
\                        /
 ------------------------
        \   ^__^
         \  (oo)\_______
            (__)\       )\/\
                ||----w |
                ||     ||
```

The `hello` is intact inside the bubble. `-n` is an option, like the `-i` we
gave `cp` and `rm`.

## More than two

A pipeline is not limited to two commands. Each `|` hands its output on to the
next one, however many there are:

```session
$ date | figlet | cowsay -n
 __________________________________________________________
/  __  __                  _                 _ _____       \
| |  \/  | ___  _ __      / \  _   _  __ _  / |___  |      |
| | |\/| |/ _ \| '_ \    / _ \| | | |/ _` | | |  / /       |
| | |  | | (_) | | | |  / ___ \ |_| | (_| | | | / /        |
| |_|  |_|\___/|_| |_| /_/   \_\__,_|\__, | |_|/_/         |
|                                    |___/                 |
|   ___  _   ____  _____  ____  _  _     _   _ _____ ____  |
|  / _ \/ |_|___ \|___ /_| ___|| || |   | | | |_   _/ ___| |
| | | | | (_) __) | |_ (_)___ \| || |_  | | | | | || |     |
| | |_| | |_ / __/ ___) | ___) |__   _| | |_| | | || |___  |
|  \___/|_(_)_____|____(_)____/   |_|    \___/  |_| \____| |
|                                                          |
|  ____   ___ ____   __                                    |
| |___ \ / _ \___ \ / /_                                   |
|   __) | | | |__) | '_ \                                  |
|  / __/| |_| / __/| (_) |                                 |
| |_____|\___/_____|\___/                                  |
\                                                          /
 ----------------------------------------------------------
        \   ^__^
         \  (oo)\_______
            (__)\       )\/\
                ||----w |
                ||     ||
```

Three commands, read left to right: ask the time, draw it in large letters,
put the drawing in a speech bubble. None of them knows about the other two.

A command that takes text in, changes it, and passes text out is called a
**filter**. That is the second word in the title of this chapter. `figlet` and
`cowsay` are both filters, which is why we could join them in either order and
put a third command in front of them.

A filter does not have to sit in the middle of a pipeline. It is the shape of
the command that makes it a filter - text in, text out - not where it happens
to stand. `date` is not a filter: it pays no attention to what is given to it,
which is why it can only ever be the first command in a pipeline.
